question: A child who ingested a large paracetamol overdose and appears clinically improved with resolution of nausea and vomiting between 24 and 72 hours post-ingestion is entering a phase of genuine recovery and no longer requires N-acetylcysteine therapy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Phase II apparent recovery (24–72 hours) is a clinical trap, not true recovery. NAPQI continues to deplete glutathione and cause hepatocellular injury during this period. Peak hepatic damage occurs in Phase III (72–96 hours). NAC therapy must not be discontinued on the basis of symptomatic improvement during Phase II.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Incorrect — this statement is false. The apparent clinical improvement between 24–72 hours is Phase II of paracetamol poisoning, characterised by transient symptomatic recovery while NAPQI-mediated hepatocellular necrosis is actually progressing silently. This is a well-recognised clinical trap. N-acetylcysteine must be continued, and liver function tests monitored closely, because severe hepatotoxicity (Phase III) peaks at 72–96 hours.
